RBI’s historic rupee defence indicates 97 per dollar is central bank’s line in the sand

Rupee surged more than 1% Monday, pulling away from the 97 level—which has emerged as a key marker for currency traders as it sits just beyond record low of 96.9650 reached in May.

Pratigya Vajpayee ,  Ruchi Bhatia  and  Anup Roy

12 October, 2026 08:38 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Indian rupee banknotes arranged for a photograph at general store in Mumbai, India, on Wednesday, July 20, 2022. Photographer: Dhiraj Singh/Bloomberg

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

India’s most aggressive currency defense in more than a decade is telling market watchers that the central bank is prepared to pull out all the stops to keep the rupee from weakening beyond 97 per dollar.

The Reserve Bank of India on Saturday announced sweeping measures to support the currency, among its toughest since the 2013 taper tantrum. The rupee surged more than 1% on Monday, pulling away from the 97 level — which has emerged as a key marker for currency traders as it sits just beyond the record low of 96.9650 reached in May.

“It is absolutely evident now that 97 per dollar is the RBI’s line in the sand for the rupee,” said Abhishek Upadhyay, an economist at ICICI Securities Primary Dealership Ltd. in Mumbai. The RBI’s message is that the rupee’s fall has been too sharp and the central bank is willing to do whatever it takes to prevent a new record low, he said.

Show Full Article

The forceful intervention follows the RBI’s first interest-rate increase in nearly four years and hawkish commentary last week, which did little to alter the currency’s course. It also shows that elevated oil prices and persistent foreign outflows from local stocks are keeping policymakers on guard against further depreciation.

The RBI wants to curb speculative bets by pushing market participants to pare positions in the forwards market and prohibit trades without real demand, according to people with knowledge of the matter, who asked not to be identified as the discussions are private.

The rupee rose to 95.5938 a dollar on Monday. It is still down about 6% this year, one of the worst performers in Asia. RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said last week the currency was undervalued on some gauges, and that markets can be irrational in the short term.

The central bank again intervened in the onshore market on Monday to support the rupee, traders familiar with the matter said.

‘Bad Optics’ Australia & New Zealand Banking Corp., Crédit Agricole SA and Malayan Banking Bhd also view 97 as a crucial level for the rupee. The RBI did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment on the matter.

Given its proximity to the rupee’s record low, 97 has become a key level for hedging and trading decisions, said Sajal Gupta, head of forex and commodities at Nuvama Institutional desk. “I think 97-98 levels should be protected because 100 would be like bad optics.”

The RBI’s new measures include a special window to meet state-run oil companies’ dollar needs and a reserve requirement on certain foreign-exchange derivatives. Banks and other Indian foreign-exchange market participants asked the central bank to relax these and delay their implementation, according to people familiar with the developments.

Meanwhile, bonds slumped on Monday, with the benchmark 10-year yield rising to the highest level since March 2023, after the RBI also asked banks to put aside more cash as part of a reserve requirement on a daily basis, and announced an open-market sale, where it sells bonds it already owns.

“The reputational risk is not so much a weaker rupee, but the perception that investors cannot rely on efficient and predictable access to currency hedging,” said Rajeev De Mello, global macro portfolio manager at Gama Asset Management SA. “Over the medium term, that could prove more damaging to foreign investors’ appetite for Indian bonds than allowing the rupee to adjust to the global energy shock.”

The measures introduced are the latest attempt by RBI to support the rupee. Earlier this year, it limited daily net open positions for banks at $100 million and barred lenders from offering clients non-deliverable rupee contracts, a restriction it later rolled back. It also removed taxes on bond investments by global funds later.

Then, in June, the RBI sought to bring in capital flows through a diaspora deposit program. That raised a record $133 billion, swelling its foreign exchange reserves to nearly $800 billion in early September. Since then, the stockpile has fallen $51 billion, partly due to its efforts to support the rupee.

While the oil window will remove some dollar demand from companies in the market, it will further drain the RBI’s reserves, said Dhiraj Nim, FX strategist at ANZ in Mumbai.

What Bloomberg Strategists say:

“The Indian rupee needs more than a series of stop-gap measures to fundamentally put it on a more resilient trajectory. The more-than-40% surge in Brent crude since the start of the Iran war and a 5% loss in the value of the rupee since then have raised India’s import bill. So, unless the country can address the trade deficit, the rupee will continue to stay under pressure beyond today’s gains.”

— Ven Ram, cross-asset strategist.

The latest steps target demand in the foreign-exchange derivatives market. For the first time, the RBI introduced a FX risk reserve, requiring lenders to hold with the central bank the rupee equivalent of 20% of the notional value of each derivative transaction above $2 million. The People’s Bank of China has a similar tool to manage pressures on the yuan by varying the reserve requirement on forward contracts.

“The RBI still has a lot of policy measures it can introduce to prevent the rupee from falling past 97,” said Eugenia Victorino, head of Asia strategy at Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken in Singapore. “It is likely hoping that these measures buy them time until oil prices pull back yet again.”

–With assistance from Bhaskar Dutta.

Authors: Pratigya Vajpayee, Ruchi Bhatia and Anup Roy

Wall Street bets big on India as IPO boom, private equity and retail investing reshape markets

Blackstone expects its India assets to double to $100 billion in coming years. That’s a sign of the growing sophistication of the financial markets within this $4 trillion economy.

Preeti Singh ,  Ranjani Raghavan ,  Saikat Das  and  Siddhi Nayak

12 October, 2026 08:34 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Blackstone Group COO Jonathan D. Gray stares into the distance. | Photographer: Jose Sarmento Matos/Bloomberg

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

Across India’s small towns and bustling cities, retail investors have been snapping up shares of newly listed companies. It’s a boom that Blackstone Inc.’s President Jon Gray celebrates thousands of miles away in his Park Avenue office.

“For us, outside of the United States, India is the most liquid market — the easiest place to get an IPO done in the world this year,’’ Gray said in an interview. India already saw one of its biggest ever initial public offerings in recent weeks and a listing with a market value of more than $100 billion is possible from billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s empire, making the country one of the world’s busiest IPO markets.

Gray and other financial heavyweights acknowledge challenges like rising inflation and the falling rupee. Yet, between its private equity and real estate businesses, Blackstone has listed a string of companies over the past decade in India and revenue growth has been high, Gray said. The firm expects assets under management in the South Asian country to double to $100 billion in the coming years.

Show Full Article

That’s a sign of the growing sophistication of the financial markets within this $4 trillion economy as it opens up further to foreign money. It’s also a dramatic turnaround from just a few years ago when private equity investors had limited options to exit investments in India, let alone at substantial profits. Now private equity, private credit and sovereign wealth funds are committing ever deeper pools of capital, while market makers like Citadel Securities LLC and hedge funds like Millennium Management LLC have built a presence there. Other parts of the financial industry are also changing swiftly.

India’s markets remain a fraction of China’s by size. High corporate taxes and the rupee’s decline leave foreign firms smaller profits to repatriate into dollars. On the political front, a youth protest movement is creating new pressures for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government.

Wall Street bosses are still looking at the economy’s long-term prospects. Many are betting on a series of measures taken by the Modi administration to jumpstart a vast digital payments ecosystem. Millions of Indians are now putting their savings into financial markets for the first time. As new developments reshape Indian finance, here are some of the biggest changes and challenges emerging:

Banking Boom In recent months, a string of Wall Street bosses have landed in India to court businesses and the government. Citigroup Inc.’s Jane Fraser had a meeting with Modi. JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s Jamie Dimon met the country’s finance minister. Both firms are working on the IPO of Ambani’s digital services giant Jio Platforms. That company is expected to go public later this year at a valuation that could make it India’s largest ever, Bloomberg News has reported.

Banks have been bolstering teams in investment banking and capital markets. Goldman Sachs Group Inc. has injected at least $500 million into its India banking franchise in recent years, Bloomberg News has reported. It’s also one of the banks on the Jio IPO.

“Rapid financialization of household savings is creating a durable pool of domestic capital to support private-sector investment,” said Sonjoy Chatterjee, chairman and chief executive officer of Goldman Sachs India.

The average fee paid to bankers in India has risen to 1.86% of an IPO’s value, according to capital-markets data provider LSEG. That’s higher than roughly 1.5% in Hong Kong.

The firms are all vying for a larger slice of the pie in what’s become one of the world’s most competitive investment banking markets. The Wall Street banks are competing against each other as well as Japanese ones and local firms like Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. and Axis Bank Ltd., who command deep client relationships and pricing power.

Meanwhile, global banks are seeing other opportunities. Citi’s India CEO K. Balasubramanian said in an interview that the bank sees added opportunities to do business with local and foreign corporations as India enters into more trade deals with countries including the UK. The India arm of Japan’s Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group Inc. plans to expand its rupee-bond business as companies diversify funding, according to a spokesperson. It has managed about 57 billion rupees ($600 million) of local bonds since the inception of its business in September 2025 and aims to significantly enhance its share over the next two to three years. The firm is also expanding in India’s IPO market.

Private Equity Money Until the 1990s, India was almost completely closed to foreign capital, and few private equity funds were involved in major deals. As the economy has opened up, PE firms have invested tens of billions of dollars and deal sizes have been increasing.

Brookfield Asset Management Ltd.’s CEO Connor Teskey says that over the next five years the firm’s investment in India will be more than $100 billion from about $30 billion in 2025. It’s a bet on “India’s immense scale, strong economic growth, respect for capital and growing demand for infrastructure,” he said.

Firms like Brookfield and Blackstone are also betting on the country’s real estate markets. Office space has seen a boom as local and foreign companies scramble for room in swanky new towers in cities like Mumbai and New Delhi.

“The one challenge obviously has been higher inflation rates and currency depreciation,” Gray said. Despite that Blackstone has had very good success in areas like its logistics portfolio because “there’s so much underlying demand that you can make up for the fact that the currency’s been going down,” he said.

Global Capability Centers The basic back-office centers that began in the 1990s have evolved into mission-critical cogs of global finance. India had more than 1,800 Global Capability Centers in 2025 and that is projected to exceed 2,400 by 2030, according to a Dun & Bradstreet report.

While low-end jobs have been shifting to places like the Philippines, the sprawling Indian campuses house armies of quants, risk analysts, investment and tech staff.

GCCs are estimated to have generated around $100 billion in revenue last fiscal year. They have grown so much that some Wall Street giants have more employees in India than anywhere else outside the US. JPMorgan alone has around 60,000 people working at its India GCCs.

Minting Millionaires Only a small percentage of people in this nation of nearly 1.5 billion people are presently invested in markets, despite recent improvements. Indians save $500 billion annually in financial assets and almost 50% of that is still in cash and deposits, according to analysts at Macquarie.

More of their money may now flow overseas. In recent weeks, India’s market regulator has said it will allow a $463 billion segment of its portfolio management industry catering to wealthy individuals to invest in overseas securities and short equity options.

India’s population of ultra-high-net-worth individuals is forecast to rise from about 19,000 in 2026 to roughly 25,000 by 2031, underscoring its growing role in the global wealth landscape, according to a Knight Frank report. That’s enabled established international private banks like Standard Chartered Plc and HSBC Holdings Plc to build sizeable franchises.

For more, read: Young, Rich, Family Office. Indian Heirs Worry Their Elders

Still, the wealth boom has brought a new set of problems for Modi. As one section of Indian society has grown richer, inequities have deepened and sparked social upheaval. Youth discontent burst into public view this year through the Cockroach Janta Party, a movement that began as satire after a Supreme Court judge compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches. As young people took to the streets  this weekend, the authorities imposed unprecedented restrictions in New Delhi, deploying thousands of police and asking telecom operators to suspend internet services near protest areas. Restrictions across dozens of major roads and intersections were in place in the capital on Monday.

Mixed Markets While longer term investments have poured in, India’s markets have taken a hit this year as the oil importing country’s currency has slumped and inflation has risen with higher crude prices. Foreign portfolio institutions have pulled out about $30 billion from domestic stocks so far this year in pursuit of artificial intelligence opportunities elsewhere.

While India is among the worst-performing equity markets in 2026, its capital markets have deepened and matured rapidly since the pandemic, underpinned partly by sticky domestic flows, the IPO boom and wide-ranging investment opportunities.

Growing liquidity and institutional participation continue to make the country an important destination in global portfolios. High frequency trading desks run by firms like Optiver Holding BV are going head-to-head with newly minted Indian trading joints and are fueling a fight for top talent. At some high frequency firms, interns have begun to command $31,000 in monthly pay in India.

Regulatory Challenges New dilemmas are emerging for India’s regulators as its markets become more liquid. Indian retail traders lost more than $9 billion trading equity futures and options in the year ended March.

That’s pushed India’s regulators to clamp down on a boom in the options and futures market, one of the most lucrative areas for foreign trading desks.

The regulator recently accused a small Mauritius-based JPMorgan unit of executing manipulative stock trades in India. The offshore unit’s trading ban has since been lifted. Last year, in one of its most dramatic actions on a foreign firm, SEBI accused Jane Street of market manipulation, an allegation that the US financial giant has denied. The firm has pressed ahead with its case in a high-profile appeal against India’s securities regulator.

GIFT City Rises A new free market oasis called GIFT City is seeing a boom. Gujarat International Finance Tec-City is part of Modi’s push to develop a hub in India that can compete with major international cities. Foreign banks are seeing assets surge in this alternative low-tax center on India’s west coast. There, they are helping set up treasury operations for corporations, offering financing for international businesses and helping foreign clients trade. HSBC has built a $23 billion balance sheet in GIFT city in under six years, according to people familiar with the matter. Citi’s assets there are likely to reach $3 billion by the end of 2026 from about $350 million last December, its India CEO K. Balasubramanian said.

The hub is “central to the internationalization of India’s economy and to building a global financial hub onshore,” he said. “That makes it a big focus for Citi.”

–With assistance from Rajesh Mascarenhas, Baiju Kalesh, Anto Antony and Samie Modak.

(Updates with added details on New Delhi)

What Trump’s Russian diesel deal means for US, surging global prices & Indian refiners

The US has eased sanctions on Russian diesel to address fuel-price pressures, raising questions over its Russia policy and the outlook for Indian refiners.

Udit Bubna

12 October, 2026 06:27 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

File photo of Russian President Vladimir Putin with his American counterpart Donald Trump | Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: US President Donald Trump’s decision to bring Russian diesel back into the American market has raised questions about Washington’s sanctions policy against Moscow and its efforts to curb revenues funding the war in Ukraine.

Trump’s decision comes ahead of the November mid-term elections, with diesel prices near record levels. Diesel is essential for trucking, agriculture and heating in the US, making higher fuel costs a concern for households and businesses.

The announcement on Friday came less than a month after Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which provides for tariffs of up to 100 percent on goods from countries that continue to buy Russian oil and gas under specified conditions.

Show Full Article

On 9 October, the US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued General License 135, temporarily authorising specified transactions involving Russian-origin diesel until 7 April 2027, allowing the proposed trade to proceed.

However, analysts are sceptical that the additional volumes will significantly ease global diesel shortages or bring down prices across markets.

Abu Dhabi-based commodity analyst Natalia Katona said the arrangement appeared to be directed at a specific regional market rather than the global diesel shortage. “The US Atlantic coast, particularly New York and the wider Northeast, has a persistent diesel shortfall because it lacks sufficient refining capacity.” .

Regular seaborne imports of around 200,000-300,000 barrels per day help meet that shortfall, Katona said.

“While many in the market argue that these volumes won’t solve the global diesel shortage, Trump is addressing a very specific local problem: diesel prices in the traditionally Democratic Northeast ahead of the elections,” she told ThePrint.

Also Read: India’s now importing pre-conflict levels of Gulf crude; share of Russian oil lowest since April

Sanctions relief versus pressure on Russia Trump’s move highlights the contrast between the US easing restrictions on its own proposed Russian diesel imports and threatening penalties against other major buyers of Russian energy.

America-based energy strategist and geopolitical analyst Umud Shokri said the arrangement was administratively permitted under the US licence, but actual deliveries would depend on available Russian supplies, export rules, shipping and payment arrangements. He also noted that some US lawmakers had questioned whether the move conflicted with federal law.

Russia’s own restrictions could pose another constraint. Moscow extended its diesel export ban for producers until 31 October, citing the need to stabilise domestic fuel supplies. Meanwhile, Ukrainian drone attacks continue to disrupt Russian refining capacity.

Despite restrictions on diesel exports, Russia continued supplying some foreign markets during the sanctions period through government-to-government arrangements which was exempt from its export ban, Katona said. These shipments included supplies to Mongolia, Kyrgyzstan and other Central Asian countries.

Shokri said there was no indication that Russian refineries returned to peak operating levels. In September, half of Russia’s six largest diesel-producing refineries had significantly reduced or halted output following drone damage, he said.

Under Trump’s supply arrangement, Russia is expected to ship 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and one million tonnes in December, according to Katona.

These volumes would be equivalent to around 75,000 barrels per day (b/d), 125,000 b/d and 250,000 b/d, respectively, averaged over a month. The December shipment could cover almost all of the US Northeast’s regular diesel import requirement of 200,000-300,000 b/d.

However, high freight rates and a shortage of clean-product tankers could limit the wider impact, as diesel markets have become increasingly regional.

Russia, according to Katona, last supplied diesel to the US in 2022, with arrivals peaking at 210,000 tonnes in December that year. No cargoes have arrived since 2023.

What it means for India’s oil trade For Indian refiners, the bigger risk lies in changing regional trade flows and potential pressure on export margins rather than direct competition from Russian diesel in the US.

India exported 630,000 barrels per day (b/d) of diesel in September, of which Europe took 280,000 b/d. These shipments had largely been contracted one to two months earlier, Katona said.

The outlook will depend on whether China resumes larger diesel exports and how shipping costs to Europe evolve.

“If China starts flooding the Singapore and Southeast Asian markets, India will have no option other than to re-orient flows towards East Africa and Europe,” Katona said.

China’s planned return to diesel exports has already pushed down refining margins in Singapore to $64-65 per barrel, she added. If shipping costs to Europe remain high, Indian refiners may find it more profitable to sell their diesel in Asian markets instead.

Shokri said a possible recovery in Russian diesel production and exports could increase competition for Indian fuel, particularly in Europe, where shipments grew in September. The greater availability of Russian diesel could narrow price premiums and compress Indian refiners’ margins, he said.

The scale of the impact will depend on how much Russia can produce and export, given continuing refinery damage and export restrictions.

For India, the key variables are Chinese exports, Russian supply, regional diesel margins and freight rates. These factors will determine where Indian fuel can be sold most profitably as shifting trade flows and sanctions reshape the global diesel market.

(Edited by Tony Rai)

Features

Surfing hotspots around the world are more vulnerable to climate change, says new study

The research analysed 57 surf breaks across eight countries to arrive at its findings. Each of the sites selected is incorporated into a World Surfing Reserve.

Purvi Rajpuria

12 October, 2026 04:43 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Representative image (c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2024

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: Many of the most prominent surf breaks across the world are vulnerable to climate change, even as the degree and type of vulnerability differ widely, a recent study found.

The study, titled ‘ Globally significant surf breaks are vulnerable to climate change ’, was co-authored by Dan R Reineman of California State University Channel Islands, along with researchers from Save The Waves Coalition and World Surfing Reserves .

The research analysed 57 surf breaks across eight countries to arrive at its findings. Each of the sites selected is incorporated into a World Surfing Reserve (WSR)—“a status applied for by local stakeholders and designated by an international non-profit organization based on each site’s cultural, historical, and environmental significance for surfing,” the study explains.

Show Full Article

These surf breaks, the research found, are vulnerable to climate change, due to changing tide levels, hardened shorelines caused by manmade structures, and shifting sands. Surf breaks rated at most risk include Croyde beach in north Devon, UK, and Oriente Salvaje in El Salvador.

What are surf breaks? Dan Reineman, a co-author of the study, pointed to the several factors that come together to form a surf break. “Surf breaks are incredibly unique oceanographic phenomena – a confluence of all these factors that fit together just right to make the wave happen – and so those processes are really sensitive,” he said .

Some of these factors include swell direction, tide, and intricate combinations of sea-floor shape. Climate change, global warming, and changing rainfall patterns can affect any of these factors, hampering the delicate balance of surf breaks and thus destroying the wave.

Significantly, the study found that coastlines that were more natural and less populated by manmade structures could adapt better to the changes caused by climate change. These coastlines were able to adapt by shifting inland and relocating sediments. Construction of features such as sea walls, jetties and groynes made the beaches and waves less resilient, Reineman said .

Also read: Mamdani has a new target. Subscriptions that make cancellations difficult

Affects local economy at large Climate change-related vulnerability matters not only to surfers, but also to the local people who depend on the multi-billion-dollar surf economy that exists in these sites.

Adam Hall, a co-founder of the North Devon WSR, was one of the local surfers who contributed to the study. Explaining the significance of surfing to the local economy, he said , “Surfers will come throughout the year. They fill up the pubs, restaurants and car parks when the swells are good in January, February and March, where if you go to any other tourist destination that doesn’t have surf, they’re dead on their knees.”

Many of these sites often have little else in terms of local economy.

Local surfers also played a key role in guiding the research. Trent Hodges, a co-author of the study and a senior programmes manager at Save the Waves Coalition, said , “We learned directly from the local surfers how they are seeing their waves change. It’s a canary in the coalmine too – when a wave changes, that often means the beach is changing, and everybody enjoys the beach.”

The study also hypothesises that similar risks could affect other surf breaks, not included in the present research, and encourages other local people and organisations to assess their vulnerability.

(Edited by Ratan Priya)
